events.what: The Times reported that US officials had investigated Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, concluded she was passing intelligence to Beijing, and found she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia denied anything unusual: a spokesperson said meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job, and Huang told Bloomberg the Megaspeed dealings were normal. He did not admit the infidelity for another ten days.
events.caveats: This row is the espionage story, not a confession: the affair was alleged by officials and denied by the company until 8 November. It is also the least clean line on the page, in a way the market control does not fix. Nvidia was already falling after a record close of $239.24 on 6 October, and on 5 November it lost 9.3% in a rout that began with AI capital-expenditure fears; the broad market fell 4.4% that day, so most of Nvidia's slide was its own sector, not the tape, and subtracting the index removes only about three of the 21.6 points this line gives back by 10 November. Read the whole first fortnight as one entangled move in which the affair arrived already inside a falling stock.

events.what: In an email to staff published as a press release, Huang wrote: "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did." He added that his family "bears no responsibility for my choices", and tied the affair to the national-security concerns in the news reports. The board announced an independent investigation by independent directors with outside counsel and, in the same breath, said it had confidence in his leadership. Three days later he was gone.
events.caveats: Sunday evening release, so the first session that could trade on it is Monday 9 November, off Friday 6 November's close of $186.64. Reported weekend and pre-market numbers circulating at the time (a 3.4% out-of-hours fall, a 6% pre-market fall) are not closes and are not drawn here. Nvidia closed 4.3% lower on the first session while the market rose 2.4%, so the versus-market view is worse than the raw one, not better.

events.what: The Times reported a second, separate extramarital relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice-president of health care, one of roughly sixty executives reporting directly to Huang, filmed being affectionate with him at a San Jose hotel in March; Nvidia's security staff asked the bystander to sign a non-disclosure agreement. That evening the WSJ reported the board was preparing to oust him. At 08:48 ET next morning Nvidia announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately: CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones was appointed the board's first-ever chair, and a search for a permanent successor opened.
events.caveats: The Powell relationship is reported, not admitted, unlike the first. The 11 November reporting and the 12 November resignation were priced in one session: the Times reached Huang by phone during Wednesday, and the WSJ and board news came after the 16:00 close, so Wednesday closed UP 2.9% and all the damage printed Thursday. Widely quoted 7.5-9% figures for 11 November are after-hours prints, not closes. Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 on Tuesday 17 November, just outside this window, so later sessions mix succession risk with results.

events.kindLabel: affair with a subordinate; forced out
events.what: Boeing's 68-year-old president and CEO, brought out of retirement to clean up the company's procurement scandals and married fifty years, was asked by the board to resign after an internal and outside-counsel investigation found he had conducted a consensual relationship with a Boeing executive, Debra Peabody. The probe found no harm to the business, no effect on her career or pay and no misuse of company resources, but the board chose "zero tolerance on breaches of ethics" and he left immediately, with CFO Jim Bell interim. His wife filed for divorce days after the story became public; he later married Peabody.
events.caveats: The closest structural analogue to Nvidia in this set: a founder-figure, an acknowledged breach of a conduct code, an immediate exit and an interim from within. The market's reaction was negligible, which the Seattle Times noted on the day, and Boeing's ethics crisis of the period (the Air Force tanker loss, the Druyun/Sears convictions) was the bigger story in the tape. Note the interim CEO, Jim Bell, died in office in October 2005, which is a separate and much larger shock to this line after the 126-session window drawn here.

events.what: HP's board forced out its chairman and CEO, the most admired operator in the company's history, after an independent investigation into a complaint by Jodie Fisher, a former event contractor who alleged sexual harassment, and into a confidential settlement paid to her. The investigators found the sexual-harassment policy had not been violated, but that Hurd had filed inaccurate expense reports to conceal the relationship and the payments, which the board said had no legitimate business purpose. He resigned immediately, not for cause, with about $12.2m in severance and the CFO as interim.
events.caveats: Read this row as a governance and honesty case, not a romance: both Hurd and Fisher denied a sexual relationship, and the board's stated ground was false expense reporting and the concealed payment. If a strict definition of infidelity is applied, this case does not belong on the page and is kept only because the concealed relationship is what the market reacted to. Big confounders: HP reported preliminary third-quarter results and raised its outlook the same morning, and the Autonomy tender offer dominated HPQ in early September. HP's own price series is split- and spin-off-adjusted, so absolute levels here are not the 2010 prints.

events.kindLabel: a rival pays the disgraced CEO
events.what: Three weeks after HP forced him out over the concealed relationship and the settlement, Oracle announced it had hired Mark Hurd as co-president and a director. Larry Ellison made the argument explicitly: "Mark did a brilliant job at HP and I expect he'll do even better at Oracle." HP sued in Santa Clara County to stop the move on non-compete grounds, and settled three weeks later.
events.caveats: The one row on this page where the affair made the stock go up. Oracle's gain is not a verdict on infidelity so much as on a scarce operator's sales record: markets priced Hurd's distribution and cost discipline, not his marriage. Announced Monday 6 September, a market holiday, so the move prints on Tuesday 7 September, when Oracle rose $1.34, or 5.9%, to $24.26 while the market fell 1.1%. HP was down about 1% the same session, roughly with the market and nothing like a punishment for the lawsuit it had just filed.

events.kindLabel: tabloid scoop on the founder's affair
events.shrug: It was still 22% higher six months on. The finding is not that investors approve of affairs; it is that with the founder in the chair, the strategy intact and the numbers unchanged, a tabloid scoop carried no information the model needed.
events.what: Hours after Jeff Bezos and his wife MacKenzie announced on Twitter that they were divorcing after twenty-five years, the National Enquirer published a four-month investigation into the affair itself, with Lauren Sánchez, drawing on texts and photographs it had paid her brother $200,000 for. Amazon issued no statement and the board took no action; Bezos remained CEO. Five weeks later Bezos went public with private messages between himself and American Media's chairman David Pecker, accusing the company of extortion over the coverage and raising the possibility that its interest in him was political, since he owns The Washington Post.
events.caveats: The flat first session is the point of this row, but the framing has to be exact: Amazon was NOT near a record when the story broke. Its all-time closing high was 4 September 2018 and it traded about 19% below that on 9 January 2019, having been crushed in the December 2018 and January 2019 technology selloff, with a government shutdown, layoffs reporting and presidential attacks on the company all in the same weeks. A market that shrugs at a founder's affair during a drawdown is a slightly different finding from one that shrugs at a record high. Two credible outlets split the publication date between 9 January online and 10 January on the newsstand; a third dates the affair story to 21 January, which is not reconciled.

events.what: Intel's board investigated a consensual relationship between its CEO and a female employee, which had begun around 2015 before Intel adopted an anti-fraternisation policy, and concluded that Krzanich had violated company policy. He resigned as CEO and director on 20 June, announced in an 8-K at 11:22am ET on 21 June, with CFO Bob Swan named interim. Wikipedia describes the relationship as an extramarital affair; Krzanich had married Brandee Krzanich in 1998.
events.caveats: The filing itself gives no reason for the departure, so the relationship is known from the reporting and the board's findings, not from the disclosure. Intel's 8-K states that the board "has determined that Mr. Krzanich's conduct violated Intel's policy prohibiting employees and directors from having consensual romantic or sexual relationships with other employees or directors". This row also sits in the worst possible operational moment for Intel — the 10nm delays, the Meltdown and Spectre disclosures and the controversy over Krzanich's own $24m November 2017 option sale — and Bob Swan's permanent appointment and the chip cycle dominate the following six months.

events.kindLabel: affair confirmed by an ethics probe
events.what: Kubasik was Lockheed Martin's president, chief operating officer and the announced successor to chairman and CEO Robert J. Stevens, who was to retire at the end of 2012. An internal ethics investigation then confirmed that he had conducted a long-term extramarital affair with a subordinate employee. On 9 November 2012, before the handover could happen, Stevens asked for and received his resignation.
events.caveats: He was the incoming chief executive rather than the sitting one, so this row measures something slightly different from the others: what it costs to lose a succession that had already been announced. The market's answer on the day was nothing at all, 0.1%, and the stock was only 3.6% below the pre-story close at its worst in six months. But that six-month window is the worst possible one for a defence contractor: the fiscal-cliff deal on 1 January 2013, fourth-quarter results on 31 January, and the sequestration cuts on 1 March, after which this line is 14.1% behind the index. The affair cost Lockheed nothing in the tape; Washington did the damage, and the versus-market view is the only way to see the two apart. Kubasik returned as chief executive of L3Harris and was dismissed there in 2026 over a second relationship allegation, charted separately.

events.what: Fourteen years after Lockheed Martin removed him over a confirmed affair with a subordinate, Kubasik was fired as chief executive of L3Harris Technologies on 16 August 2026 for conduct inconsistent with the company's code of conduct. The company did not publish the details; Semafor and the Wall Street Journal reported that an independent ethics investigation had focused on allegations of an inappropriate relationship with an employee and aggressive, profane behaviour. His spokesperson denied that a relationship with a subordinate was the cause.
events.caveats: This is the only repeat episode in the set, and the least substantiated: the company's own statement names no relationship, the allegation comes from two news reports of an unpublished investigation, and the executive denies it. It is drawn because the comparison with 2012 is the point — a board that had already been through this once, at a company whose shares were listed both times — not because the affair is established. Read the 2026 line as an allegation with a firing attached.
